network.overall_strategy: Construct an atom-balanced, conditional network with ten distinct reaction-node sequences, not ten independently demonstrated prebiotic syntheses. Three carbon-feedstock branches converge on valine precursors: acetone-derived cyanosulfidic chemistry, propanal/formaldehyde aldol chemistry, and isobutanol dehydrogenation. Aldehyde-derived branches can enter Strecker chemistry through cyanohydrin or imine intermediates; these are alternative entry sequences within the same reaction family, not independent mechanisms. Aminonitriles subsequently undergo either direct hydrolysis or hydantoin formation followed by hydrolysis. The ten listed pathways comprise two acetone-derived routes, four aldol-derived routes, and four alcohol-derived routes. Unsupported prebiotic applications and the particularly uncertain cyanosulfidic chain-extension step are explicitly marked speculative. The supplied review is not accepted uncritically: its C6 aminonitrile would hydrolyze to leucine, not valine; its chain-extension equation omits nitrogen-containing products; and its achiral chemistry does not establish selective L-valine production. Those errors are not propagated. Organic feedstock availability remains a boundary assumption. Reactions require separate compatible environments rather than a single mixed reactor. Neutral molecular formulas represent connectivity, with protonation controlled by local pH. Hydrolysis nodes explicitly describe lumped amide intermediates. A null environment_formed denotes either an externally supplied feedstock or, for valine, formation in more than one environment.

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous pool; mildly alkaline conditions provide some cyanide while retaining HCN. Concentration and protection from rapid volatilization are required; UV is not required for this addition.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to the acetone carbonyl followed by protonation produces the tertiary cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: This is chemically conventional cyanohydrin chemistry and is the acetone-entry reaction attributed to Patel et al. (2015) in the supplied review. No mineral is needed. Equilibrium, HCN loss, and competing cyanide chemistry limit accumulation; the review does not establish a general environmental yield.

reactions.name: Sulfide addition to acetone cyanohydrin nitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic sulfide-containing solution, approximately pH 8-9; H2S and HS- are represented by their neutral parent species.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrosulfide attacks the nitrile carbon; proton transfer and tautomerization generate the thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review attributes this nitrile-to-thioamide transformation to Patel et al. (2015). H2S is a consumed reagent, not an unexplained catalytic agent. Cyanohydrin dissociation and competing sulfide reactions remain relevant; substrate-specific rates and yields are not independently verified here.

reactions.name: Hypothetical cyanosulfidic deoxygenative homologation and cyanide trapping
agents: Cu(I)-cyanide photoredox complexes, proposed for this specific transformation

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-irradiated cyanide/sulfide solution; staged chemistry rather than an assumed one-pot process. Copper speciation, sulfide precipitation, and sulfur-product speciation require experimental determination.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved net sequence requiring removal of the tertiary hydroxyl functionality, conversion of the original thioamide carbon into an aldehyde-equivalent carbon, loss of the original nitrogen as ammonia, and capture by a new cyanide. Elemental sulfur is an idealized terminal oxidation sink; transient polysulfides are not resolved.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE: the supplied report attributes a related transformation to Patel et al. (2015), but its displayed equation loses nitrogen and cannot establish the proposed mechanism. This replacement is atom-balanced with inferred coefficients and explicitly includes ammonia, but balancing does not demonstrate feasibility. The first cyanide-derived carbon becomes the eventual valine alpha carbon; the second becomes its carboxyl carbon. Cu(I) photoredox catalysis is chemically distinct from claiming dissolved elemental copper. Aldehyde formation, productive reduction, sulfur products, and selectivity must be demonstrated. This is the decisive unresolved bottleneck for P1 and P2.

reactions.name: Crossed aldol addition and dehydration of propanal with formaldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic alkaline pool, approximately pH 9-11; concentration cycles may favor condensation. Mixed-product formation is expected rather than selective methacrolein production.

reactions.mechanism: Propanal enolate adds to formaldehyde, producing a hydroxymethylated aldehyde that dehydrates to methacrolein. This node represents the net aldol/dehydration sequence.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE as a prebiotic feedstock-supply reaction; it is not supported by the supplied Patel et al. (2015) review. Standard crossed-aldol chemistry provides a carbon-conserving way to construct the required branched C4 skeleton. Propanal self-condensation, formaldehyde disproportionation, repeated hydroxymethylation, and polymerization compete. Selectivity under the stated geochemical conditions is unestablished.

reactions.name: Candidate selective hydrogenation of methacrolein to isobutyraldehyde
agents: native Ni-Fe alloy surface, such as awaruite, as a candidate hydrogenation catalyst

conditions.other: Anoxic, locally sulfide-poor rock-water interface with accessible metallic sites; effluent must cool before downstream cyanide chemistry.

reactions.mechanism: Surface activation of hydrogen followed by addition across the carbon-carbon double bond would preserve the aldehyde group and produce isobutyraldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE: no substrate-specific prebiotic demonstration is supplied. Ni-containing metallic surfaces are chosen for hydrogen activation and alkene hydrogenation, not merely because they are minerals. The crucial unresolved issue is selectivity: carbonyl reduction, full conversion to alcohols, hydrogenolysis, and surface poisoning may prevent aldehyde accumulation. This bottleneck conditions all aldol-derived pathways.

reactions.name: Candidate isobutanol dehydrogenation to isobutyraldehyde
agents: native copper surface as a candidate heterogeneous dehydrogenation catalyst

conditions.other: Anoxic, sulfide-poor, H2-poor flowing hydrothermal zone; product removal and rapid effluent cooling are required. This is not assigned to an H2-rich serpentinization reactor.

reactions.mechanism: Catalytic removal of hydrogen from the alcohol O-H bond and adjacent C-H bond forms the aldehyde and molecular hydrogen without molecular oxygen.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE geochemical application of an established alcohol-dehydrogenation reaction family; the supplied research does not document this reaction. Copper here is a solid catalyst, not dissolved Cu(0) or an unspecified stoichiometric reductant. H2-rich conditions oppose dehydrogenation, while sulfide can deactivate copper. Adequate isobutanol supply, reaction rate in water, and aldehyde survival remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Isobutyraldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Anoxic concentrated solution, approximately pH 7-9; retention of volatile aldehyde and HCN is necessary. Shaded pore water can limit photochemical destruction between irradiation episodes.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to isobutyraldehyde followed by protonation gives the C5 alpha-hydroxynitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is a conventional cyanohydrin entry to Strecker chemistry. The supplied review describes the same C5 hydroxynitrile downstream of its proposed cyanosulfidic branch, but does not independently demonstrate this aldehyde-supply route. Its integration here is therefore speculative relative to the supplied evidence. The reaction preserves the isopropyl branch and introduces the future carboxyl carbon without any chain shortening.

reactions.name: Net conversion of the valine cyanohydrin reservoir to aminonitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich anoxic solution, approximately pH 8-10; sufficient cyanide activity and volatile retention are needed. The cyanohydrin, aldehyde, and imine pools interconvert.

reactions.mechanism: The cyanohydrin equilibrates with aldehyde and HCN; ammonia forms an imine or iminium species, and cyanide capture yields the aminonitrile. The displayed reaction is the balanced net conversion, not direct displacement of an unactivated hydroxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015), as summarized in the supplied review, motivates this cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile connection. The review's simple hydroxyl-substitution explanation is replaced by the chemically appropriate Strecker equilibrium mechanism. This entry shares imine chemistry with rxn_009 and rxn_010, so the resulting graph paths must not be represented as independent reaction families. No enantioselection is supplied.

reactions.name: Isobutyraldehyde-ammonia imine formation

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich anoxic solution undergoing concentration; imine is a transient equilibrium species rather than an assumed isolable reservoir.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde to form a carbinolamine, followed by reversible dehydration to the imine.
reactions.reasoning: Imine formation is part of classical Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850), although that historical precedent does not establish this specific prebiotic setting. This explicit aldehyde-entry branch is not demonstrated in the supplied review and is speculative as an environmental pathway. Aqueous imine concentrations may be low; subsequent cyanide trapping, rather than imine isolation, must pull the sequence forward.

reactions.name: Cyanide trapping of isobutyraldimine

conditions.other: Anoxic imine/iminium-HCN equilibrium mixture with ammonia present; proton-transfer equilibria determine the reactive species.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the imine or iminium carbon, followed by proton transfer to give the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the defining carbon-carbon bond-forming step of the classical Strecker reaction family (Strecker, 1850). Its proposed geochemical implementation remains speculative relative to the supplied evidence. The branched aldehyde provides the correct valine side chain, and cyanide supplies the eventual carboxyl carbon. Attack on either face produces a racemic precursor.

reactions.name: Direct aminonitrile hydrolysis to valine

conditions.other: Acidic volcanic-water setting, approximately pH 1-2, reached after aminonitrile formation; prolonged residence may be necessary. Ammonia and valine are substantially protonated under these conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration to 2-amino-3-methylbutanamide and amide hydrolysis forms valine and releases the nitrile nitrogen as ammonia. Two water molecules are consumed per aminonitrile, with coefficients omitted from the graph as required.
reactions.reasoning: This is the standard Strecker hydrolysis connection described in the supplied review in association with Patel et al. (2015). It does not establish efficient hydrolysis in ordinary cool pools: residence time, acid availability, and competing degradation are important bottlenecks. The C5 aminonitrile gives C5 valine without carbon loss. The supplied C6 aminonitrile alternative is excluded because ordinary hydrolysis instead gives leucine.

reactions.name: Carbonation and cyclization of valine aminonitrile to hydantoin

conditions.pressure: approximately 1 atm, with sustained dissolved inorganic carbon supply
conditions.other: Anoxic ammonia/ammonium-containing concentrated solution with CO2-bicarbonate-carbonate equilibria; approximately pH 8-10. Conditions are separate from strongly acidic nitrile hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Aminonitrile carbonation produces a carbamate-related intermediate, followed by intramolecular reaction at the nitrile and rearrangement to the hydantoin. Net incorporation of CO2 gives the balanced cyclic product without adding a third nitrogen.
reactions.reasoning: The Bucherer-Bergs reaction family provides laboratory precedent for hydantoin formation from carbonyl/cyanide/ammonia/carbonate systems (Bucherer and Steiner, 1934). SPECULATIVE as a prebiotic extension: it is not documented in the supplied Patel et al. (2015) review, and environmental rates and yields for this aminonitrile are unestablished. It is included as a chemically distinct sequestration and release route, not as evidence that carbonate necessarily improves valine production.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening and decarbamoylation to valine
agents: hydroxide and hydronium in successive hydrolysis stages

conditions.catalyst: general acid/base catalysis in separate stages
conditions.other: Anoxic hot-water circulation; alkaline ring opening followed by conditions permitting cleavage of the N-carbamoyl group. Transport from the surface hydantoin-forming compartment and subsequent cooling are conditional requirements.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic ring opening forms N-carbamoylvaline; subsequent ureido-group hydrolysis releases valine, ammonia, and CO2. Two water molecules are consumed overall. The expelled carbon is the extra carbonate-derived carbon, not a carbon removed from the valine skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin hydrolysis is an established amino-acid preparation strategy, but this particular natural hydrothermal implementation is SPECULATIVE and unsupported by the supplied review. Hydantoins and N-carbamoyl amino acids can be persistent, so stronger conditions are assigned rather than assuming facile ambient hydrolysis. Natural pH sequences, residence times, transport, and competition with valine degradation require validation. No enzyme or chiral catalyst is assumed.

pathways.name: Acetone-cyanosulfidic entry with direct nitrile hydrolysis
pathways.description: Acetone enters the reviewed cyanohydrin/thioamide branch, followed by the explicitly speculative C5-forming conversion, Strecker equilibration, and direct hydrolysis. Feasibility depends critically on rxn_003.

pathways.name: Acetone-cyanosulfidic entry with hydantoin-mediated release
pathways.description: The acetone branch supplies aminonitrile, which is carbonated and cyclized before hydrothermal release of valine. This route inherits the unresolved cyanosulfidic conversion and adds conditional hydantoin formation and hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Aldol-derived aldehyde through cyanohydrin and direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Propanal and formaldehyde conditionally supply methacrolein, whose selective hydrogenation supplies isobutyraldehyde. Cyanohydrin formation, net ammoniation, and nitrile hydrolysis then yield valine.

pathways.name: Aldol-derived aldehyde through cyanohydrin and hydantoin
pathways.description: The conditional aldol/hydrogenation branch enters the cyanohydrin reservoir. Its aminonitrile product proceeds through hydantoin formation and staged hydrolysis rather than direct nitrile hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Aldol-derived aldehyde through explicit imine capture
pathways.description: Aldol-derived isobutyraldehyde reacts first with ammonia. Cyanide traps the transient imine, and direct aminonitrile hydrolysis yields valine. This is an alternative Strecker entry sequence, not a separate Strecker mechanism.

pathways.name: Aldol-derived imine capture with hydantoin-mediated release
pathways.description: The conditional aldol branch supplies aldehyde for imine-first Strecker chemistry. The resulting aminonitrile is routed through hydantoin rather than directly hydrolyzed.

pathways.name: Alcohol-derived aldehyde through cyanohydrin and direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Conditional anaerobic isobutanol dehydrogenation supplies isobutyraldehyde. Cyanohydrin equilibration and ammoniation provide the aminonitrile for direct hydrolysis. A sufficiently H2-poor aldehyde-producing environment is essential.

pathways.name: Alcohol-derived cyanohydrin with hydantoin-mediated release
pathways.description: The speculative alcohol-supply branch feeds the cyanohydrin entry to Strecker chemistry. Carbonation and cyclization divert its aminonitrile through hydantoin before valine release.

pathways.name: Alcohol-derived aldehyde through imine and direct hydrolysis
pathways.description: Isobutanol conditionally supplies the branched aldehyde, which enters imine-first Strecker chemistry. Direct hydrolysis of the resulting C5 aminonitrile yields racemic valine.

pathways.name: Alcohol-derived imine capture with hydantoin-mediated release
pathways.description: Conditional alcohol dehydrogenation is followed by imine formation and cyanide capture. Hydantoin formation and staged hydrolysis provide the alternative target-release sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The intermediates have the correct carbon counts, and the terminal aminonitrile would yield racemic valine. However, rxn_003 remains a major mechanistic gap: its balanced equation does not establish the required deoxygenation, thioamide conversion and cyanide incorporation. Treating rxn_008 as an equilibrating Strecker reservoir conversion is appropriate. Surface conditions for completing rxn_011 are unspecified.
suggestions: Resolve rxn_003 into atom-mapped mechanistic steps and provide evidence for its redox driver, catalyst if required, sulfur products and selectivity.
Specify sulfide activity and cyanohydrin stability for rxn_002.
Provide a staged pH, temperature and residence-time protocol supporting both Strecker conversion and complete nitrile hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin branch does not resolve the unsupported carbon-skeleton transformation in rxn_003. Aminonitrile carbonation and hydantoin formation are consistent with Bucherer–Bergs-type chemistry, but their operation under the proposed surface conditions is not established. Hydantoin hydrolysis can yield valine, although a hydrothermal label alone does not establish complete ring opening and decarbamoylation.
suggestions: Validate the substrate-specific transformation in rxn_003 before treating this as an operational route.
Specify dissolved inorganic carbon speciation, pH and temperature for rxn_012.
Demonstrate hydantoin transport and hydrolysis through the N-carbamoyl intermediate to valine, including competing decomposition and incomplete conversion.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The crossed aldol/dehydration constructs the correct methacrolein skeleton, and the downstream cyanohydrin/Strecker sequence is chemically coherent. The principal bottleneck is rxn_005: selective alkene hydrogenation while retaining the aldehyde is plausible with suitable catalysts, but no appropriate mineral phase or operating conditions are supplied. Complete surface nitrile hydrolysis and preservation of reactive aldehydes during transfer also remain conditional.
suggestions: Specify aldol catalyst, pH and feed ratios, with evidence that crossed condensation competes successfully against propanal self-condensation and other side reactions.
Identify an environmentally credible catalyst and hydrogen fugacity for rxn_005, measuring aldehyde retention and competing alcohol formation.
Provide transfer, concentration and hydrolysis conditions that preserve the intermediates and complete conversion to valine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a valid conditional carbon-skeleton route with a recognizable hydantoin endpoint. Its main limitations are the unvalidated selective hydrogenation in rxn_005 and insufficient conditions for hydantoin formation and subsequent complete hydrolysis. The lower confidence relative to direct hydrolysis reflects these unresolved chemical requirements, not the additional environment transfer or reaction count.
suggestions: Establish crossed-aldol selectivity and substrate-specific methacrolein hydrogenation under the proposed conditions.
Provide primary experimental support for formation of 5-isopropylhydantoin from the stated aminonitrile and carbon dioxide system.
Specify hydrothermal pH, temperature and residence time, demonstrating valine recovery rather than accumulation of partially hydrolyzed products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Explicit imine formation and cyanide capture give a mechanistically appropriate Strecker sequence. The imine need not accumulate as an isolated compound, but its transient formation and trapping must compete successfully with hydration and hydrolysis. This pathway is effectively tied with P3 because both share the same upstream hydrogenation bottleneck and downstream aminonitrile hydrolysis requirements.
suggestions: Specify catalyst and operating conditions establishing selective rxn_005 rather than assuming hydrothermal hydrogenation preserves the aldehyde.
Describe imine formation and cyanide capture as coupled equilibria, with ammonia activity, cyanide speciation and water activity constrained.
Demonstrate the transition from Strecker-compatible conditions to a hydrolysis regime that releases valine without excessive decomposition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The imine-capture sequence and hydantoin connectivity are chemically appropriate. Nevertheless, rxn_005 lacks an established selective catalyst/environment combination, while rxn_012 and rxn_013 lack conditions demonstrating productive hydantoin formation and complete release of valine. This is an alternative sequence within the same Strecker-based branch, not independent experimental confirmation of the network.
suggestions: Validate the aldol and selective hydrogenation sequence with realistic catalysts and competing-product measurements.
Quantify transient imine capture and subsequent carbonation under explicitly compatible conditions.
Track hydantoin ring opening, N-carbamoyl intermediate conversion and valine survival during hydrothermal treatment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Once isobutyraldehyde is available, the downstream sequence is credible Strecker chemistry. The limiting step is rxn_006: aqueous isobutanol does not undergo useful selective dehydrogenation merely because it is heated hydrothermally. A suitable catalyst and favorable hydrogen activity are required; hydrogen-rich conditions would oppose the stated direction. Surface hydrolysis conditions are also missing.
suggestions: Specify the dehydrogenation catalyst, temperature, pressure and hydrogen fugacity, with evidence for aldehyde selectivity.
Quantify hydrogen removal or physically justified coupling to the hydrogen-consuming rxn_005 zone; a shared hydrogen node alone does not establish thermodynamic coupling.
Demonstrate aldehyde transfer and a subsequent hydrolysis regime that yields recoverable valine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The structural sequence reaches the correct hydantoin and could ultimately yield racemic valine. However, selective alcohol dehydrogenation remains unvalidated, and the hydantoin branch requires additional evidence for carbonation and complete hydrolysis under the stated environments. Neither an atom-balanced dehydrogenation equation nor a hydrothermal label establishes productive conversion.
suggestions: Establish a low-hydrogen-activity catalytic regime for rxn_006 and quantify competing alcohol or aldehyde reactions.
Specify carbonate speciation and temperature for productive hydantoin formation.
Provide transport and residence-time constraints demonstrating hydantoin hydrolysis to valine before substantial decomposition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The transient imine and cyanide-trapping steps are appropriate for forming the valine aminonitrile. They do not remove the unresolved catalyst and hydrogen-management requirements of rxn_006. This pathway is effectively equivalent in confidence to P7, since the cyanohydrin and imine entries are related equilibrating routes within the same Strecker chemistry.
suggestions: Provide substrate-specific evidence for hydrothermal isobutanol dehydrogenation and identify the hydrogen sink.
Constrain ammonia concentration, pH and cyanide availability so transient imine capture outcompetes reversal.
Specify physically justified aldehyde transfer and separate hydrolysis conditions, including product recovery measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pathway identifies appropriate aminonitrile and hydantoin intermediates, but target production remains conditional on selective alcohol dehydrogenation and complete hydantoin hydrolysis. The explicit imine entry is mechanistically reasonable but does not constitute independent evidence relative to P8. Compatible conditions and intermediate survival across the proposed settings have not been demonstrated.
suggestions: Establish the catalyst, energy input and hydrogen-removal mechanism supporting rxn_006.
Demonstrate aminonitrile formation followed by hydantoin formation under specified, compatible solution conditions.
Quantify hydantoin hydrolysis kinetics, intermediate accumulation and valine stability under the proposed hydrothermal conditions.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally strong: all 20 molecule nodes and 13 reaction nodes are connected, molecule IDs are consistent, and the ten listed sequences lead formally to the correctly identified racemic valine target. Accepting the deterministic balance check, there are no mass or charge violations. The reported coefficients should be made explicit for rxn_003, rxn_011 and rxn_013; the multiplier required by S8 is not intrinsically suspicious. Chemical viability is nevertheless conditional. rxn_003 lacks a demonstrated mechanism, while the alternative carbon-entry branches depend on unvalidated selective hydrothermal hydrogenation in rxn_005 or dehydrogenation in rxn_006. Established Strecker and hydrolysis chemistry supports the endpoint but does not establish productive operation of the complete network. Surface and Hydrothermal labels do not specify pH, temperature, catalyst phases, hydrogen activity, energy input, residence times or physically justified transfer. Separate compatible settings are acceptable; their number and order are not penalized. Literature alignment is partial: the network correctly rejects the review's C6-to-C5 hydrolysis claim and unsupported L-selectivity, and transparently labels speculation. These are justified corrections, not departures deserving a penalty. However, the internally inconsistent review and its citation to Patel et al. (2015) cannot establish every proposed transformation; reaction-level primary evidence and conditions remain missing. Feedstocks are accepted as declared boundary inputs, not demonstrated supplies. P3 and P5 are effectively tied as the strongest conditional routes, with P3 selected as a representative. Overall confidence reflects shared bottlenecks and integration evidence, not pathway count. The network does not meet the 0.9 approval threshold.
